cases.abstract: Imitation policies trained on few expert trajectories can fail when their errors carry the robot into undemonstrated states. DMD addresses this mismatch by creating supervised recovery examples, pairing synthesized wrist-camera views away from demonstrated poses with corrective action labels. A pose-conditioned diffusion model is adapted from pretrained weights using task demonstrations, task-agnostic play, or both. Labels target a later expert pose because a sampled displacement may overshoot the next frame, causing a next-frame label to command backward motion. Policies then learn jointly from real and generated image-action pairs. Real-robot evaluation covers pushing, stacking, pouring, and shirt hanging. In ten apple-pushing trials per method with 24 demonstrations, DMD achieves 100% success, compared with 30% for behavior cloning and 50% for a replicated NeRF-based augmentation method. With eight demonstrations and play-trained view synthesis, success is 80%, versus 20% for behavior cloning. Augmenting a diffusion policy trained on 1,447 cup-arrangement demonstrations raises success from 4/25 to 16/25 on unseen cups in an unseen environment; both policies use center-cropped, rectified images. These results support corrective augmentation beyond scarce-data training, provided deviations remain recoverable rather than involving irreversible events such as spilling contents.
cases.methods: DMD augments not only what the policy sees but also how it should act after a local deviation. A pretrained latent diffusion model is fine-tuned on image pairs and their relative camera transforms, recovered from task or play trajectories through structure from motion. At generation time, a sampled pose displacement specifies a virtual wrist-camera position, and the model synthesizes the corresponding view. Composing transforms from that virtual position to a later expert pose supplies a corrective action label. The future target matters because a perturbation can overshoot the next demonstrated pose, making a next-frame label command backward motion. On pushing, angular prediction error approximately plateaus at the third future frame, so that frame is used for labeling. Joint training on real and generated pairs therefore supplies recovery supervision absent from the original trajectories, rather than relying on visual diversity alone.
cases.results: A modest offline error reduction accompanies a marked online success gain on apple pushing. Adding diffusion-generated examples to color jitter and flips lowers median angular error from 0.355 to 0.328 radians, while policies trained on 24 demonstrations succeed in 100% of DMD trials versus 30% for behavior cloning, over ten trials per method. This contrast is compatible with accumulated errors making small prediction differences consequential, but does not isolate that mechanism. Play data are useful without being required: task-only view-model training yields 80% pushing success, compared with 100% using task and play. Pouring also favors DMD, at 80% versus 0% with task-and-play training and 70% versus 30% with task-only training. However, these are separate randomized A/B comparisons whose conditions, including lighting, may differ; the pouring numbers do not establish a play-data advantage. The supported benefit is learning corrections for recoverable deviations, not reversing spilled contents.
cases.notes: Abstract and Methods retain the pose-to-label relationship (III-C; Fig. 5): later targets avoid backward labels after overshooting. Results compare offline error with online success (Tables I-II) without identifying error accumulation as an isolated cause. Low-data pushing uses a play-trained view model; the large-data cup test retrains both policies on center-cropped, rectified images. Pouring contrasts remain separate A/B tests (Table IV), not a matched play-data ablation. Recoverability is an assumption, not guaranteed by synthesis.

cases.abstract: Fine bimanual manipulation requires demonstrations collected through responsive hardware and policies that sustain precision over long action sequences. ALOHA and Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) address these coupled requirements. ALOHA is an open-source teleoperation system built within a USD 20,000 budget, using 50 Hz joint-space leader-follower control and customized parallel-jaw grippers. ACT predicts chunks of joint targets to shorten the effective horizon, but combines overlapping predictions at every step so sequence prediction need not discard feedback. Conditional variational training accommodates variation in human demonstrations. The main evaluation covers two simulated and six physical tasks; physical training uses 50 demonstrations per task, except 100 for velcro threading. In 25 physical evaluations per method with one training seed, ACT records 88% success at the bag-opening stage and 96% at battery insertion; four tuned baselines score zero at both stages. Ablations distinguish the contributions of chunking and generative training, while a six-person study finds faster teleoperation at 50 Hz than at 5 Hz. Performance remains uneven: reported velcro-insertion success is 20%, and initial candy-unwrapping evaluation yields 0/10 completed attempts.
cases.methods: ACT groups future joint targets into chunks while retaining frequent observation updates. On ALOHA, inputs comprise four camera views and current follower-arm joint positions, but supervision uses leader-arm targets: their offsets from follower positions determine the forces produced by the motor controllers. Predicting a sequence rather than a single step reduces the effective horizon and can capture temporally correlated behavior such as pauses within a chunk. To avoid the abrupt updates of executing an entire chunk before observing again, deployment queries the policy at every step. Predictions for the same execution time are combined with exponential weighting, smoothing transitions while incorporating feedback. Training uses a conditional variational autoencoder to represent variation across demonstrations, with a latent inferred from demonstrated actions and joint observations and regularized toward a Gaussian prior. At deployment, that encoder is discarded and the latent is fixed to zero.
cases.results: The ablations distinguish a sequence-prediction benefit from a benefit specific to variable demonstrations. With temporal ensembling disabled, ACT's mean success across two simulated tasks with scripted or human data rises from 1% for single-step prediction to 44% for 100-step chunks; longer chunks slightly worsen performance. BC-ConvMLP and VINN also improve with chunking, supporting its usefulness beyond the transformer architecture in these settings. By contrast, removing conditional variational training barely affects scripted-data performance but reduces the human-data mean from 35.3% to 2%, linking its value to demonstration variability. Temporal ensembling is not uniformly beneficial: separately tuned configurations improve ACT by 3.3 percentage points but reduce VINN from 37% to 17%. Visual precision remains a difficulty in physical tests: reported velcro success drops from 92% at lifting to 20% at insertion despite 100 demonstrations. Candy unwrapping gives 0/10 completed attempts initially; later, 3/5 candies are unwrapped with ten attempts allowed per candy. That change in retry budget precludes reading the latter figure as a single-attempt improvement.
cases.notes: Abstract preserves hardware and policy co-contributions (III-IV). Table II reports 96% pinching after 92% grasping for Slide Ziploc; clarify the stage-count definition. Opening and insertion are described as final-stage outcomes, not joint trajectory completion. Methods retains same-time ensembling (IV-A) and leaves the reconstruction norm unspecified because pseudocode and implementation text differ. Results anchors chunking, CVAE and separately tuned ensembling to Fig. 9; candy evaluations retain distinct retry budgets (Appendix F). Four-baseline comparisons cover two detailed physical tasks; the other four compare only with BeT.
